item.title: The company that almost built the iPhone died because it didn't believe it had any constraints
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cautionary-差点做出-iphone-的公司-死于不认为自己有约束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cautionary-差点做出-iphone-的公司-死于不认为自己有约束/
item.description: General Magic had the biggest industry alliance in history, more money than it could spend, and the best engineers alive — and sold 3,000 devices in six months. It lacked neither money nor talent. What it lacked was any sense that it had constraints.
item.content:encoded:
General Magic had the biggest industry alliance in history, more money than it could spend, and the best engineers alive — and sold 3,000 devices in six months. It lacked neither money nor talent. What it lacked was any sense that it had constraints.

Tim Harford walks through a complete case of "everything was right and it was all wrong," and the second half — two rounds of eliminating the causes of failure — is worth more than the story itself.

4:28 The iPhone was imagined in 1989
While at Apple's Advanced Technology Group, Peratt used a large red notebook to describe a future information and communication product: it should bring personal satisfaction like jewelry, have perceived value even when unused, offer the comfort of a touchstone, the feel of a shell, the magic of crystal. What he drew was a smooth rectangle, no buttons, only a touchscreen, able to serve as a phone, a messaging device, a portable TV and a game console, and able to book plane tickets. It was 1989: most cell phones were the size of a brick, Apple's new portable computer weighed 16 pounds, and the World Wide Web did not yet exist. He called the idea a pocket crystal, imagining people carrying it everywhere — "if your house caught fire, you'd think, first save the family, then grab my pocket crystal." He told Bill Atkinson, and Atkinson brought in Andy Hertzfeld, two of the core programmers behind the original Macintosh.

9:40 A company with no product can still make Wall Street line up
General Magic had no profits, no revenue, not even a product — only an idea — and it issued stock to ordinary retail investors. Goldman Sachs bankers shoved each other to grab allocations; one banker asked, "What's it going to take? Would it help if I took off my shirt?" and then actually did, standing half-naked in the conference room. The stock doubled immediately after listing. Each partner in the alliance had already put in several million dollars. As one vice president in the book told David Epstein, they had so much money they never had to worry about making payroll — what startup never has to worry about making payroll? That is the key mechanism: enough money that you never have to make a trade-off.

12:46 The tech was so good it made a partner's department obsolete on the spot
Two young engineers flew to Japan to show a hardware prototype to Mitsubishi. The demo had barely started when the host suddenly called in a group of employees in work clothes, apologized, and asked them to start over — because this thing had no modem, it was all implemented in software. A groan came from the audience, and a manager named Kato slumped forward and put his head on the table. The host apologized again: "You just made Kato's department obsolete." This technology made answering machines, arcades, books, keyboards and mice obsolete. At the same time they built a precursor to USB, a new programming language called Telescript, called portable networking the cloud, put skeuomorphic icons on a touchscreen, and built a store where you could buy applications — back when nobody called it an app store.

17:55 They built the future but not a product
The first device running the General Magic operating system was Sony's Magic Link in 1994. Behind the gorgeous graphics it was hard to use, shipping with a 200-page manual; it was the size of a hardcover book, its grayscale monochrome touchscreen only the size of a postcard, and it ran on old-fashioned AA batteries that drained alarmingly fast. No Wi-Fi, no Bluetooth — the body had only an old-style telephone jack, so sending messages and making calls both meant sitting at a desk and plugging into a phone line. It didn't even have a built-in phone. In today's purchasing power, about $1,600. Sony sold 3,000 units in the first six months, mostly to friends and family of General Magic employees. A few years later, Apple sold roughly 300,000 iPhones on day one. In 1995 Motorola's Envoy had wireless communication, but cost nearly twice as much as the Magic Link.

20:00 eBay's idea was dismissed by a colleague as the dumbest thing he'd ever heard
Pierre, a technical support engineer at General Magic, built a webpage on the side: list the things you have sitting unused at home, let other people bid on them. He called the site AuctionWeb, showed it to colleagues, and asked whether he could spin it out as a company, or whether General Magic would invest. One colleague's response was typical: that's the dumbest idea I've ever heard — you want strangers to trust each other on the internet? Good luck, we're not interested. This quiet man was Pierre Omidyar, and that website was eBay, which later made him a billionaire. It is also a miniature of General Magic missing the Web — people inside reminded management daily, and management always found a reason to ignore it.

24:06 Missing the Web was embarrassing, but it wasn't the cause of death
In the documentary, former employees talk about missing the World Wide Web with laughter and sighs mixed together, but Tim Harford argues this failure is a distraction. When the Magic Link launched in 1994, the Web was still a curiosity; even if it had been Web-compatible, that wouldn't have been enough to make someone spend the equivalent of $3,000 on a Motorola Envoy. The second explanation is "too early": by the time the iPhone launched in 2007, memory prices had fallen 1,000-fold since 1994, a typical microprocessor had 500 times the computing power, and there was Wi-Fi, 3G and a Web with real content. That technology gap is real, but one technology commentator in the documentary says General Magic could never have succeeded no matter what it did, and Tim says: that sounds plausible, but he's wrong.

29:19 They had time to extend the calendar back to the start of astronomical time
Epstein's argument is that General Magic had no constraints at all: the best hardware and software engineers, excellent design and marketing, a charismatic prophet-like leader, plus Apple's investment, several million from each alliance partner, and retail investors' money. With both talent and time, why compromise — just go build the pocket crystal, even if early-1990s technology couldn't possibly build it. The consequence was that nobody was forced to figure out what they were actually doing: when they described the target market they said Joe Sixpack, meaning everyone. So the product got stuffed with an instrument panel, a big walking-lemon emoji, a coin-flip animation. The coin flip came from co-founder Andy Hertzfeld, a man who at that moment clearly felt he had all the time in the world. The calendar originally covered only 1904 to 2096, a few lines of code, and it was first changed to the year 1 AD, then to the start of astronomical time.

33:33 Tony Fadell asked only two questions
Tony Fadell used to call General Magic every day begging for a job, and when the company collapsed he was heartbroken — but he learned something. At his next company he focused on just two things: given today's technology, what is new, exciting and possible? The answer was MP3s and ever-cheaper hard drives, and combining them could produce a digital music player that made Walkmans and CD players obsolete. The second question was what deadline to set himself. The answer: it's January 2001, and we ship before Christmas. The company he joined was Apple, and what shipped on time a few weeks before Christmas was the iPod — one thing done beautifully. That restraint paved the way for the next project, the pocket crystal that was actually built: the iPhone. His colleague Andy Rubin later founded Android, and others co-founded LinkedIn, ran Google Search, and led Apple's AI, Safari and Apple Watch.

item.title: The case for export controls has retreated all the way down to a single premise that still holds
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cogrev-出口管制的理由一路退守-只剩一个前提说得通/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cogrev-出口管制的理由一路退守-只剩一个前提说得通/
item.description: First it was about military use, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, then to limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.
item.content:encoded:
First it was about military use, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, then to limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.

A three-hour debrief on a China trip; the second half's analysis of the policy machinery toward China (the drift in the rationale for controls, decoupling risk, alternatives) is more worth hearing than the first half's travelogue.

8:56 What the China discourse lacks is a target state
Nathan says the missing piece in America's discussion of China is a ‘target state’: everyone jumps straight to ‘we have to win’, but nobody answers what winning looks like, what happens if we lose, or whether there is an achievable condition for victory. His target is Pax Machina, or better, Pax Robotica — the two countries and the world sharing the prosperity and peace of the AI era, robots going into factories, into fields, into homes, while avoiding the AI version of the sword of Damocles. He says explicitly this is not about winning, it is about arriving together. A competition with no target state leaves only escalation itself.

18:56 China isn't rising, it's returning to historical normal
On the claim that ‘China can't innovate’, Nathan uses one word: cope, and says it is isomorphic to cope in the AI field — conceding that AI has gotten this far, but insisting it won't reason, won't discover new knowledge, won't change paradigms. His judgment is that China's return is the long-run historical norm, and that the period he and Dario grew up in — China down, America the sole superpower — was the anomaly. So any effort to slow China's progress can at best work short-term, and China will be a first-tier player in almost every major human domain. This is not a prediction; it is, in his view, something already locked in by historical structure.

28:44 On purchasing power, China is half again bigger than the US
In dollar-denominated GDP, the US is about 30 trillion and China about 20 trillion, so the US is 50% bigger; on purchasing power parity, China is about 45 trillion and the US still 30 trillion, so China is 50% bigger the other way. Nathan says a good meal for two in Shanghai can come in under $10, which you can't do in New York, San Francisco or even Detroit, so the PPP measure is closer to reality. A more concrete picture: a roughly 45-minute pedicure is about $12, and the young employee in her twenties at the shop pulls out an iPhone 17 — the iPhone 17 is not cheaper in China than in the US, and high-end Xiaomi and Huawei phones approach a thousand dollars. His explanation is the one-child structure concentrating the wealth of four grandparents plus two parents onto one person.

1:25:10 The chip ban hits a century of humiliation
China sees itself as a top civilization that spent most of history at the technological frontier, and that missed once and was invaded, forced to take opium, with the European powers and Japan as the perpetrators — and someone who was 20 when the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976 is still alive today. The core lesson is that you cannot fall behind at the technological frontier, ‘we are never going back’. Huawei is the tech champion under this frame: the first to genuinely reach the top of a global frontier industry, only to be blocked by the US pressuring allies over espionage risk, when Snowden has already proven the US listens to everyone. The chip ban is the same script replayed: AI is barely off the ground, there isn't even an agent that can reliably book a flight, and the sale is banned first. Nathan says this is not Xi Jinping's view alone; it has seeped into educated society. He also concedes that American companies' grievance over stolen IP is entirely legitimate.

1:35:23 China doesn't talk about an AI race, it talks about public goods
Nathan did not hear a single person the whole trip say China is ahead, that China will win, and almost nobody even framed AI as a race; what he heard was prosperity, material abundance, how to care for an aging population. In a mall he asked a car-selling company about autonomous driving, and they volunteered that ‘but Tesla is better’. At WAIC, the first line of Xi Jinping's speech was that this field began at Dartmouth College in the US — he could have left it out, and careful observers read it as an olive branch; another line was that we should jointly oppose ‘over-extending the concept of national security in the AI field’. The hardest signal China has put out so far is open weights: take them, run them for free, fine-tune them however you like, and once they're out you can't take them back. Nathan says this is both a sincere wish and a strategic position, quite credible now, but entirely capable of changing later.

2:11:27 The rationale for export controls keeps retreating
Nathan thinks export controls do have an effect, but mainly in the future — the large-scale expansion of chip capacity hasn't landed yet. What he really objects to is the drift in the policy rationale: originally preventing military applications, then retreating to stopping frontier models, now retreating to limiting how many AI agents China can run; that sounds like trying to suppress the Chinese public, keeping Chinese companies and individuals from using the tools Americans use themselves. The only self-consistent premise for this policy is a belief that we are in a short race toward godlike superintelligence and that whoever gets there first takes all — which is basically Anthropic's belief, so Dario advocating these policies is not self-contradictory; he genuinely believes recursive self-improvement kicks off in '27 or '28. Nathan concedes he can follow the logic, but still argues for slowing the frontier together instead.

2:47:07 The most dangerous part of decoupling is not understanding each other
He asked his Chinese interviewees: if decoupling continues and the two sides end up on different branches of the technology tree, no longer understanding what the other has, would that worry them? The answer was ‘not yet’; when would it? ‘When China's chip ecosystem is good enough that we can do our own thing entirely’. From this he derives the core risk: a hardware fork drags along a hardware-algorithm co-design fork, and add to that China stopping open weights and stopping publishing in English, and in not too long a time you could reach ‘we don't know the shape, architecture or capabilities of the other side's AI’. At that point both sides would genuinely be right to panic, and genuinely right to race.

3:07:25 Replace the arms race with a disease gold-medal table
He first lays down a rule: don't train LLMs to maximize money-making on the open internet, and don't train AI to accomplish military objective x by any means necessary — that is training by hand the very takeover we fear most. The alternative is a ‘disease-cure gold-medal table’: China and the US both love medal tables, and Olympic-style competition is a positive-sum game. The table could be most cancer types cured, most diseases cured, highest energy-density battery, lowest annual traffic deaths. He says this needs very little capital to catalyze and could be offered unilaterally as a global public good. The landing point: he doesn't care whether the cancer cure comes from China or the US, he just wants cancer cured.

item.title: You Can't Build Superintelligence Inside a Data Centre: The Bottleneck Is Real-World Signal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.description: Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.
item.content:encoded:
Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.

Tom Reed pushes the argument that ‘signal is sovereign’ all the way to the end, and it will change how you judge AGI timelines and AI lab strategy; the analogies are sharp and the density is high.

2:54 The bottleneck for the singularity is signal, not compute
Tom's positive claim is not that superintelligence is impossible, but that it cannot be stacked up inside a data centre. His mechanism: to be good at solving problems, you need a source of problems, and that source can only be hard interaction with the real world in serial time. He compresses this into one line — ‘signal is sovereign’ — bodies need pain, companies need profit, models need real deployment. So he judges that the arrival of superintelligence depends on deploying AI into the economy expensively, painfully and slowly, not on how much more compute gets stacked up inside a lab.

5:01 Jaggedness will not disappear before the singularity
The current way capabilities advance does not support the claim that ‘the model is accumulating a general g’: models only get better at the things they have a chance to practise, so the capability boundary is more uneven than anyone expected. In 2016 nobody would have predicted a model that beats Stanford Law graduates on the bar exam but cannot play tic-tac-toe reliably. Tom thinks jaggedness is mainly a product of the training data distribution, and there is no reason to believe automating AI R&D would end it, so he proposes Toner's Law: we should expect jaggedness to persist longer than expected, even after we have adjusted for it.

6:01 Patchwork RL will not buy you general intelligence
Tom fixes on the current toolbox for capability progress: custom RL environments are the main engine. In Mechanize's telling, each environment is a single engineer spending a week patching one specific failure observed on a real frontier model; in Zhengdong Wang's telling, scaling used to hand you a bundle of capabilities at once, and now they have to be unlocked one by one with effort. Tom's challenge: are we really going to do the singularity one problem per week at a time? If RL really generalised, AI companies should have shown evidence by now; when Dwarkesh kept pressing Dario, every one of Dario's rebuttals was just a weak analogy between RL and the pretraining generalisation of the GPT-2 era.

8:26 For most tasks the relevant data is zero
The common rebuttal is that LLMs are wildly sample-inefficient and could improve enormously, and AI bulls point smugly at DeepSeek reaching GPT-4 level on a fraction of the compute. Tom does not buy it: Anson Ho and Beren Millidge both point out that gains in intelligence per FLOP come mainly from data quality rather than algorithm quality, and pure algorithmic innovation yields fairly weak returns at constant compute. More fundamentally, for most tasks the relevant data simply does not exist — improving sample efficiency by orders of magnitude still multiplies zero. His test: if the internet had never existed, how much progress could today's talent and compute make on writing code? His guess is tens of billions of human-hours.

11:40 Text about a task is not the task
For most economically interesting tasks, what is in the corpus is description, commentary or advice, not a record of performing the task itself. Dominion is a board game with a huge amount of strategy writing, yet Claude plays it badly: the training process that teaches it to write beautiful articles about Dominion is a different thing from building an agent that can win, because the optimisation target is ‘the advice looks good’ rather than ‘the strategy wins’. Tom's analogy is that the relationship between LLMs and most tasks is a bit like the relationship between McKinsey and running a company. The exception is writing code — the tokens are themselves a constituent part of the task — so training AlphaZero on chess commentary rather than chess games is the norm.

14:06 Scores go up, real capability does not
How does self-improvement inside a data centre know it has actually got stronger? Of the submissions on SWE-bench accepted by AI automated graders, close to half are rejected by the real human maintainers of the relevant codebase — scores can be pumped up while the merge rate does not move. Tom asks in return: how is Claude 8 supposed to tell, from the results of a Become-POTUS eval alone, whether its clever new algorithm really improved Claude 9's ability to become president? Evals are useful, but they are always stubbornly incomplete proxies; the only eval that ultimately counts is voters, customers, the economy and the P&L. Without those, your singularity gets ruthlessly Goodharted.

15:28 Market data is not hidden, it does not exist yet
The second layer of doubt is more fundamental and more speculative: even an arbitrarily intelligent simulator cannot generate practice data for many tasks, because that data can only be produced through interaction with the relevant market. This is Hayekian: that something is good is a signal generated by millions of actors revealing preferences through behaviour, and it cannot be simulated inside a data centre — it is not that data collection happens to fail, it is that the data does not yet exist anywhere. He uses his own board gaming as the analogy: a game of Twilight Imperium takes 12 hours, he will plan weeks ahead until he feels certain of winning, and about 5 minutes into the real game his predictive power goes to zero. Continual learning does not save you either, because without a genuinely diverse problem set you cannot tell which algorithm is better.

21:17 The winner may be the deployer itself
Corollary one: a policy focus on ‘internal deployment’ and ‘automating AI R&D’ may be misplaced — superintelligence is not impossible, it just will not arrive in the shape currently imagined, on the timeline currently predicted; the next phase looks more like the grind of deployment, customer discovery and real data collection. Corollary two: data holders have far more power than they realise (Ukraine is one example), and the asymmetry between ‘companies that can build frontier models’ and ‘entities that hold proprietary deployment data from real economic activity’ may flip. Corollary three: labs may conquer vertical industries one by one, and the way to win is to become the deployer yourself.

item.title: An Account for Every AI Agent: Credit Card Fees Can't Carry the Machine Economy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
item.description: Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.
item.content:encoded:
Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.

The segment on how Coinbase uses AI internally is the most valuable: one "brain" per service, corrections must be written back, and the mechanism is concrete enough to copy; agent payments come with hard numbers, while the new-drug section is more opinion than detail.

6:47 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents
Armstrong says agents are already generating a flood of transactions worth a few cents: VC firms scraping paywalled data for research, recruiters crawling LinkedIn, one agent calling another specialized agent as a tool to fetch source data. But the minimum per-transaction fee on a debit or credit card is a flat 30 cents plus a percentage, so the old rails basically don't work below $1 — paying 30 cents to move 1 cent makes no sense. The number he gives: about 76% of the agentic commerce transactions they see are under 30 cents. That is the hardest argument for stablecoins and crypto rails cutting into the machine economy.

11:42 Build a "brain" for every service
Coinbase has built a "brain" for every team, every repo, every service and even every employee: it holds every incident that service has ever had, the financial controls that must be enforced, every A/B test that has been run, the full GitHub history, and which PRs were accepted or rejected. When an agent comes to change code, it reads this brain first. The truly critical step: when a human reviewer finds the agent missed something, they are not allowed to just hand-edit and merge — that correction must be written back into the brain. That way one correction covers all future cases, and the one-shot PR rate keeps climbing, something Armstrong calls "recursive self-improvement."

15:00 The CEO runs 10 agents changing code at once
Armstrong says that now, when he hits an idea or a bug, he no longer pings the team all day — he drops the comment into an internal harness (they call it Toshi) and sends over a finished PR for review, which he says is addictive. He has also gotten the CEO back to writing features: have an expensive frontier model break a complex feature into three phases of ten items each, then have it recommend which cheaper model to use for each subtask, then run 10 agents in parallel on phase one. He says that over the course of doing this podcast, all 10 items got done and were waiting for his review.

17:02 What gets killed is tasks, not people
On whether AI will make companies smaller, Armstrong's judgment is: productivity really is rising, but that is a separate matter — what gets automated or eliminated is tasks, not people. He does not think a company like Coinbase shrinks to 10 people; rather, the people already there can do vastly more and everything speeds up; and yes, two-person and five-person companies will do volumes that were previously unimaginable. The result is that the cost curve of revenue relative to headcount changes: the same group of people produces far more, and over the long run margins should rise. He does not close the door on it — some companies will still hire at the same pace.

18:33 88% of revenue no longer comes from Bitcoin trading
Armstrong cites the numbers from the earnings report: 88% of revenue now comes from non-Bitcoin trading. The interesting part is that Coinbase's stock price is still highly correlated with the Bitcoin price. He says he loves Bitcoin, sees it as digital gold and sound money for everyone in the world, but crypto is updating every part of the financial system. The tokenized equity product he just announced is currently available only outside the US, and they are talking with regulators about a US path; he stresses that these are real stocks — backed 1:1 by real securities held in custody, not synthetics, derivatives or debt instruments.

21:57 Prediction markets are more than sports betting
Armstrong says prediction markets are growing extremely fast inside the Coinbase app: within a few months of launch they reached roughly $100 million in annualized revenue, growing more than 100% quarter over quarter. Sports is indeed part of it, and he sees that as entertainment worth celebrating — but he thinks it is much bigger than that, and that the societal implications are not yet fully understood. His example is policy: to judge whether a policy should be implemented, you could first form a prediction market on "what will the unemployment rate be one, two, three years after implementation." Further out are big questions with no clear settlement date, like "is there a God," which he calls an opinion market, with mechanics like buying a stock — you are just betting on whether it gets better or worse.

31:53 Restore cells to their youthful function
New Limit takes the epigenetic reprogramming route: it does not change the cell type (the Yamanaka-lab style approach does), it only restores the cell's youthful function. The platform first uses AI to search the vast combinatorial space of transcription factors for candidates, runs large-scale pooled screens, then does functional experiments (mostly in animal models), and finally goes into human trials. The first batch targets three cell types: hepatocytes, vascular cells and T cells of the immune system. The first Phase 1 trial is in alcoholic liver disease (ALD), where patients have almost no option besides a liver transplant and survival after diagnosis at 12 months is very low. Armstrong estimates that this one drug alone, if successful, could be worth $20 billion, but the goal is for a 40-year-old to have the liver, immune system and blood vessels of a 20-year-old.

41:10 What America lacks is not land, it's a sandbox
Armstrong's interest in special economic zones comes from a "meta-question": what is slowing down progress — in many places, overregulation. He mentions that Coinbase invested in Prospera in Honduras, and he thinks they have had ups and downs with the local government but are close to resolving it. During the campaign there was discussion of an idea called "freedom cities": the federal government holds vast tracts of land, take 10 or 100 square miles, and on that land you don't have to go through the usual EPA process — you can build data centers, nuclear power plants, unlimited drone delivery without getting FAA approval item by item — first test what works in a safe, controlled sandbox, and once it works, push it back out to the whole country through the normal process. He says the problem now is that in many cases there is simply no sandbox to test in, and if entrepreneurs can't iterate they can't solve the problem.

item.title: Inheritance of acquired traits is proven in nematodes; in humans there is no evidence yet
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.description: Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — changing only RNA in the brain alters behavior three generations later.
item.content:encoded:
Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — changing only RNA in the brain alters behavior three generations later.

35 minutes walks the whole conceptual chain from DNA to small RNAs, with experimental designs and key numbers included; on the mammalian part the speaker repeatedly states what is unknown, so it won't hand you a conclusion you can apply.

4:37 The genome is the whole book, and each cell pulls out only one page
Every cell carries the same genome. Rechavi's metaphor is that every room holds an IKEA manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out only one page, and that page is RNA, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. The messenger RNA that actually encodes protein is only a small part of RNA: less than 2% of the genome's sequence encodes messenger RNA, while a great deal of the RNA that gets transcribed does other things, many of which remain unexplained. This distinction is the foundation for everything that follows — DNA determines which instructions can be opened, and only then does the question become whether lived experience can rewrite those instructions.

11:35 Two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits
Why, by default, can't what you learn in life be passed on? Rechavi attributes it to two barriers. The first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century August Weismann proposed what is now called the Weismann barrier — only germ cells can hand information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. The second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates all kinds of chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — roughly 90% in mammals and humans. The reason for erasing is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being locked into the few pieces one room happened to make.

12:46 It was opposed and also wanted, and not entirely for data reasons
This barrier theory kept acquired inheritance out of favor for a long time. Rechavi describes two sides: one is theory, the barrier is sitting right there; the other is the atmosphere the controversy itself creates. He takes Schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — Schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, and at the same time wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: nothing you do affects the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. Rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning. But he doesn't push this into ‘because people want to believe it, it has promise’; he only says RNA is a new lead, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in the mammalian field.

16:20 Nematodes can run hundreds of generations in one PhD
Why trust nematodes? The conditions Rechavi lists are concrete: a C. elegans is always 959 cells, 302 of them neurons, and since the 1980s it has had a complete connectome, like a subway map marking who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can watch neurons fire directly, and you can switch genes on and off with optogenetics; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, raised in a dish eating bacteria, in a highly controlled environment where nature and nurture can be separated; generation time is 3 days, so one PhD can run hundreds of generations of nematodes. Under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in nematodes already has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it.

21:20 Offspring that can't make small RNAs still resist viruses
The experimental design is clean enough to read by color: use a fluorescent virus, and if the virus replicates successfully the nematode turns green, while if it is destroyed it stays black. First let nematodes be infected by a virus and destroy it, then knock out the machinery for making small RNAs in their offspring — these offspring have no ability to make small RNAs from scratch themselves. Then infect them with the same virus. If they still stay black, the only explanation is that they inherited small RNAs from their parents. That is exactly what happened: all the offspring stayed black, and the resistance could be passed on for several more generations. Sequencing can directly read those small RNAs matching the viral genome, and only offspring whose parents had been infected have them. These nematodes have no T cells or B cells; they defend against viruses with RNA, and this mechanism is RNA interference, which won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

24:46 The brain and heredity don't use the same language
The boldest question in this episode is: can the brain leave information for the next generation? Rechavi points out the obstacle is translation — the brain stores information in the three-dimensional structure of synaptic connections, while any heritable information must squeeze through the bottleneck of a single cell, the fertilized egg. He also offers another possibility: learning something might just mean removing a particular odor receptor, in which case one RNA controlling that receptor would be enough to pass it on; such phenomena have been reported in mammals, but he says they haven't been proven convincingly enough, because no one has explained how information gets from the brain to the germ cells. His own route bypasses translation: in a 2019 Cell paper, changing only the production of naturally occurring small RNAs in the nematode brain altered the foraging behavior of offspring, affecting them all the way to three generations later, with the mechanism landing on the germline gene sage-2, and also requiring the protein that physically carries RNA.

28:17 Mammals lack an RNA amplifier
Why can nematodes do it while mammals must be doubted? The mechanism Rechavi gives is blunt: the nematode's secret is that it can keep amplifying these small RNAs, so the signal doesn't get diluted. In mammals there is no known comparable amplification mechanism, so the question becomes — how does a tiny bit of RNA affect the whole organism? One possibility is that it acts only very early in development: at that point there are only a few cells, and it might even act on the placenta formed during pregnancy, after which development is steered off course step by step, and problems like metabolism follow. This is the ‘developmental origins of health and disease’ line of thinking. He also frames RNA's role in mammals as a candidate rather than a conclusion: small RNAs are the leading candidate for transmitting protective or harmful effects of stress, but ‘in mammals we don't know, and time will tell’.

31:07 RNA is more plastic than DNA, so start with diagnostics
The applications come in three layers. The nearest is diagnostics: in Israel, most couples planning to have children get DNA diagnostics for genetic diseases, but right now no one looks at RNA; if the mechanism becomes clearer, RNA would be another layer, a whole new world, and there may be certain RNAs associated with disease. The advantage is that it isn't fixed the way DNA is — DNA is yours, and if you can't change it you can only choose another embryo; RNA is plastic. Only a step further out is intervention: in rodent experiments, overfeeding causes problems in the next generation, but if the mice are made to exercise, this abnormal inheritance is corrected; when doing IVF, perhaps you could change the RNA composition of the things you introduce. Rechavi is restrained about the timeline: he says this doesn't happen now, it's science fiction, but if it gets figured out, he has also imagined telling someone preparing for IVF ‘you should go run on the treadmill for a while’, which would change your RNA profile.

item.description: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal in stores, fences strip the labels and resell, and the goods then go up on secondhand platforms. Connected goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.
item.content:encoded:
Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal in stores, fences strip the labels and resell, and the goods then go up on secondhand platforms. Connected goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.

High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorized, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the state of federal legislation, with plenty of hard numbers.

8:19 A third of shrink is self-inflicted
Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious, which Scott frames as the things we do to ourselves versus the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The industry line that has circulated for years is that of malicious shrink, roughly 40% comes from internal employees, 35% from people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages move only a few points a year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that it has been underreported ever since COVID, with neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting capturing the full picture.

22:52 Employees are explicitly told not to chase people
The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal, and these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out the door to turn them into cash — so they will get physical, and they have. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and even killed. That's why asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene, just to back off. His attitude is that he will trade shrink for human safety every single day, and management and the board will back that decision.

23:53 RFID dies the moment it enters a steel store
Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and yet in 2026 is still expensive and hard to scale. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains what's peculiar about Home Depot: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, effectively a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read and you have to use active-signal solutions. He also says tag cost is now almost zero, and the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits is extremely costly. They've tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but to do that for a single drill you'd have to rework an entire production line, and it's very hard to scale.

25:58 Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
The division of labor works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs to go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — which might be a garage, a warehouse or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store labels and electronic tags before reselling, and the money goes up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a small crew of a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backward from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

35:19 Selling one combo kit requires 4.2 restocks
Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there's a $799 combo kit that requires 4.2 restocks for every one sold. Take that to finance and they immediately understand it's a gross margin problem — as long as it breaks even or even makes a little money, locking it up pencils out. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and if they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up carefully selected categories, with a QR code to summon an associate who opens it in an average of 90 seconds; and locking up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually go up, because the product is finally there.

39:23 A fake bill of lading can just drive the goods away
On the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion, where a whole container is rerouted at the port or transload warehouse and taken elsewhere, sometimes even loaded back onto a container ship and shipped out; second, a driver drives eight hours across state lines, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and moves boxes; third, forging bills of lading and pickup documents, using AI to make the paperwork look real, and the driver pulls in, says he's there to pick up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new isn't necessarily the methods, it's the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the area that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years; cars sitting in a yard get broken into by a group, and the other side has good intelligence — they don't touch every car, only the ones carrying guns or electronics.

41:28 AI in security is an efficiency tool
Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closing and handing over to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores so the existing cameras can run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to get to the point of recognizing a combination of suspicious behaviors and then identifying a specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

44:30 Seven years ago nobody cared; now there's a federal bill
He says he's very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it's bipartisan, it has passed the House, it's attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, and the president has said he'll sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources, and the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination center. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: nobody took it seriously, and the prevailing mood was still decriminalization and defunding the police.

item.title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Has Won for Three Centuries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.description: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks America's three-century winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable framework for judgment, not news-cycle opinion.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy held itself up as a pillar of stability by ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark and the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is accelerating toward collapse.

10:00 The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through some battle; it won through a five-step playbook. First, an open society on an island — the 17th-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in. Then global trade: Dutch merchant ships sailed the world, and the wealth was so great that even the paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over Silesia, you seized India and Canada across the globe. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot live without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut it off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut off, and its economy promptly seized up.

16:38 Everything China does is to avoid having the cord cut
Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own jugular. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast — oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and the Chinese economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read side by side: on one hand building oil reserves on a scale that surprises outsiders; on the other, throwing up solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as possible. It is not schizophrenia, it is one thing: pulling out the soft spot of ‘dependence on the outside world’ one root at a time. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to feed themselves.

25:50 Every round of technology dividends needs new institutions to match
Mead starts from the ownership society: at America's founding there were independent farmers with land everywhere, and while a bridge is good it means raising my taxes — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era was matched by the Homestead Act, with the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, and a national market grew out of it; what replaced the family farm in the 20th century was the single-family suburban house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth-distribution machine. Now that machine has hit housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the ‘infrastructure’ of institutions — he coined the word info-structure, meaning the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley tilts toward the tech Hamiltonians
American foreign policy debate has been four vocabularies for centuries: Hamiltonians want a strong state clearing the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, Jacksonians stay isolationist in peacetime and fight to the death when hit. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the room. Mead says the new species truly worth noting is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no say’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, and even wants its employees to be patriotic — selling code to China is shameful, and your colleagues will report you outright. The core of business has shifted from old multinationals to tech nationalists, and this is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The power with more equipment fears technological turnover most
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time he visited a drone factory and saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; months later he went again, and the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers move together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to get the wounded out’ — you need to build a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people, with a squad of drones alongside hunting the enemy drones coming to attack. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. Things flip every six months. The bitter irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this kind of parameter revolution — existing equipment turns from an advantage into a relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has no great battle to fight, yet it is bottled up at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

54:16 The new variable most worth watching in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On ‘will the mainland attack Taiwan’, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it will cross the threshold — failure would be catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for example requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to first call at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade, doing things that change facts enough without triggering an armed US response. The real new variable on the Taiwan board is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japanese independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine and reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan turns very fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must add Japan as a factor, is the key to the Taiwan question in the next few years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe that ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain — ‘I might go soft when the time comes’ — that commitment has a crack. Automating part of foreign-policy decision-making to AI amounts to turning retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilizational scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is ‘very interesting and a little confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

item.title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.

If your image of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will overhaul it. Hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account.

8:07 What actually happens if you or I get ECT
If you or I were to receive ECT, the steps go like this: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. The next morning, in a hospital or outpatient setting, an IV line is placed and two blood pressure cuffs are put on (arm and right leg), with EKG, EEG and EMG hooked up. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant such as succinylcholine is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is inserted, and then a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, or even half a second). The goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are already relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the EEG.

14:15 Electrode placement, and why the right side comes first
There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (the way it looks in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it produces fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function sits in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side should, in theory, reduce language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During a course of treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are too much, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral isn't working well enough, switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and the effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then titrate up from a low dose until a seizure appears. But treatment doesn't stop at just reaching threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. With bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. The dose varies from person to person and has to be adjusted as you go. If in one session a patient's seizure doesn't occur or doesn't last long enough (under 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, sometimes longer.

20:22 We still don't know exactly how ECT works
Why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still don't fully understand. There are several leading hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter change: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine and GABA (the inhibitory transmitter) all shift markedly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over a course of treatment. Two, large hormonal fluctuations in ACTH, prolactin and TSH are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Three, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still has no one-to-one mechanism. The mechanisms may also differ by condition (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), so for now the only option is to keep researching.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating severe depression, ECT's key numbers are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (symptoms fully gone) of 50%-60% and response rates (symptoms clearly improved) of 60%-90%. By comparison, the best remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT has another uncommon benefit — it can cut the 30-day readmission rate in half. This is not to say it should be first choice, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not rare); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression plus severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Memory problems draw the most attention among side effects
ECT's most difficult side effects center on cognition and memory. Right after the procedure there is brief confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be declines in attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive function actually improves in the long term — possibly because the depression improves. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) mostly recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, which is why many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (losing past memories) is what worries patients more: it usually affects recall of the most recent months or even years before treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more likely to cause this than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a frequently misidentified, fatal syndrome
Catatonia is often simply lumped in as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that any psychiatric or neurological illness can trigger. Patients appear awake, eyes open, yet are almost completely motionless and mute, and may show posturing or waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position stays there). Because they cannot eat or drink and are immobile for long periods, they are prone to malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures, and even death. Untreated catatonia has a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from many causes. The girl with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis mentioned earlier (the 'Brain on Fire' case) developed catatonia, and when both immunotherapy and lorazepam failed, she ultimately recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck is not efficacy but access
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT currently faces is finding a place to get it. His hospital performs more than 6,000 treatments a year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 per patient. But it is not widely available across the US, and adults and children traveling across state lines for care are not few — especially in infants, children and adolescents with catatonia from autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely hard. Improving access is therefore his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors on other internal medicine, pediatric and critical care teams often don't recognize catatonia and don't dare, or don't think, to call an ECT consult; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is part of his daily work.

item.title: The Supreme Court Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Handed Searches and Paddlings Back to the Schools
