The method: cut off an open-source LLM's "predict the next token" head and replace it with a classification head that outputs a 0-15 AI-involvement score. Training data is built with "synthetic mirroring": take a human-written article and have an LLM compress it into a prompt ("write 200 words covering these three points"), then feed that to a random frontier model, yielding a paired human/AI sample on the same topic. The second layer is editing prompts, plus clause-level labeling: text left as-is is human, text that was changed is AI-assisted, and new sentences conjured from nothing are AI-generated.

40:00 A detector's lifeline is its false-positive rate, not its accuracy
Pangram 4's false-positive rate is about 1/24,000, measured by running millions of pre-2022 documents (an era when AI ghostwriting was essentially impossible); its false-negative rate is about 1/300, measured by taking real user prompts from WildChat and regenerating them with frontier models. Not perfect, but pointed in the right direction. Bryan's experience is that false positives are extremely rare, and that is precisely the lifeline for whether a product can be taken seriously. Pangram 4's step change came from switching a 512-token window to token-level output: a whole human-written document with two AI sentences stuck in the middle can be pointed out word by word.

46:00 A detector doesn't need to be 100%, it just needs to make cheating cost something
Max says education is a huge market, and this is the first year anyone has realized "there exist genuinely usable AI detectors." The product logic isn't 100% precision — it's creating friction on the shortcut, turning "toss the assignment to AI" from zero-cost into costly, so students take the next-easiest path, which is doing it themselves. The same judgment applies to enterprise settings: Oxide's hiring is a writing-intensive process, and an LLM-parroted "why I want to join Oxide" in corporate boilerplate is recognizable at a glance — the detector just makes it explicit.

50:00 Most "I was falsely flagged" sob stories are astroturf ads
Max distinguishes two kinds of opposition. One group genuinely wishes detectors didn't exist: it lets the AI text their profession produces be authoritatively identified. The other is marketing from the humanizer ecosystem: these tools claim to rewrite AI text so it fools Turnitin and Pangram, sold to students caught cheating on assignments; they typically also bundle an "AI detector" that first declares your text AI, then sells you the rewriting service. Many of the Reddit sob stories about "teacher falsely flagged me at 76% AI, I got a zero" are this kind of lead-gen astroturf — run them through Pangram and they come back all AI-written.

59:00 Stronger models haven't made detection harder — they've made it easier
Asked whether he's forever chasing the frontier model, Max gives a counterintuitive judgment: two things happen at once — models get smarter, but after post-training repeatedly teaches "correctness" and preferences, the output distribution is far narrower than in the GPT-2 era. GPT-2 tried to simulate the full distribution of human output; today's models only give the "correct" token, not what an ordinary person would say. He and the three Oxide hosts share the same feel: new models talk with a "strangely erudite" flavor, and detection hasn't gotten harder — it's gotten easier to pick up.

1:01:00 The next argument is how much the human actually put in
Pangram can already guess the model family internally: the probe's top-1 accuracy is 90%, but to productize it they'd need to get it to 98%. The further direction is "reverse Pangram" — inferring what prompt might have generated this text and how much context the model was given: two bullet points or fifteen? That dimension of information changes the characterization of Druckenmiller's op-ed entirely — giving five pages of notes to polish counts as collaboration, giving five bullet points to expand is ghostwriting. The next argument in detection isn't "was AI used," it's "how much did the human actually put in."

item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-eyeonai-乌克兰最大无人机商-月产近10万架-ai拦截是第一步/
item.description: Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, and its interceptors take down Russian Shaheds costing over $50,000 at a cost of about $2,000 each. AI guidance is already in combat, but full autonomy is still far off.
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, and its interceptors take down Russian Shaheds costing over $50,000 at a cost of about $2,000 each. AI guidance is already in combat, but full autonomy is still far off.

This episode is a rare case of a leading Ukrainian drone manufacturer describing directly what battlefield drones actually look like, what they cost, and where the boundaries of AI use lie. It is information-dense and directly useful for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.

4:07 Nearly 100,000 a month, and capacity is still expanding
General Cherry was founded in 2023 and initially produced only about 10 drones a month; today monthly output reaches about 100,000 (the exact figure is confidential). The company has worked with more than 110 military brigades, and its best units consume more than 5,000 drones a month. Capacity is still rising, because battlefield consumption is enormous and drones have become consumables.

7:09 Ukraine has hundreds of drone companies, but only 10-15 at the top
The number of drone companies in Ukraine may be as high as 2,000, but the vast majority are garage-scale workshops. Only 10 to 15 large companies can genuinely produce 1,000 to 10,000 units a month, and General Cherry claims to be in the top five. This fragmented but enormous industrial ecosystem is the foundation of Ukraine's rapid innovation, but it also means fierce competition.

8:14 AI models are built in-house, co-created deeply with the military
General Cherry's AI guidance system is entirely self-developed, backed by a strong R&D department, and built in close cooperation with different military units at the front. They gather battlefield feedback every day through mobile teams and iterate on products quickly. This ‘R&D-combat-feedback’ loop lets Ukrainian drone technology adapt rapidly to changes on the battlefield, rather than depending on external procurement.

10:20 The rocket-shaped FPV came from Red Bull, not Ukraine
This rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian invention; Red Bull first used it in 2021 or 2022 for sporting events. Ukrainian companies found that this shape could reach higher speeds than ordinary quadcopters, so they adopted and optimised it. This reflects the rapid learning and pragmatism of Ukraine's drone industry — it does not chase originality, only effectiveness.

17:24 A $2,000 interceptor against a $50,000 Shahed
General Cherry's interceptor drones (such as Bullet) cost about $2,000, yet can shoot down Russian Shahed drones that cost $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is Ukraine's key strategy for dealing with Russia's ‘saturation attacks’ — using cheap drones to consume the enemy's expensive assets while avoiding the waste of expensive Western-supplied air-defence missiles.

21:28 Interceptors have confirmed more than 5,000 Russian shootdowns
Since production began in February 2025, General Cherry's tactical interceptor drone (General Trajectory Air) has confirmed more than 5,000 Russian drone shootdowns, including more than 1,000 Russian ‘Moniya’ drones in December alone. The model that intercepts Shaheds also entered mass production in December 2025, with confirmed shootdowns approaching 1,000. These numbers show that interceptor drones have become an important force in battlefield air defence.

23:28 AI runs on the device, not in the cloud
General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the drone's local camera chip, not in the cloud. After an operator detects a target by radar and launches the drone, the AI automatically identifies and locks onto the target without human intervention. This on-device AI design avoids battlefield communication latency and jamming, and is the key to making it viable in real combat.

27:32 Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is now unavoidable
Marko admits that if drones became fully autonomous it would be terrifying — killing would no longer require another person, only a robot or a drone. At present they use semi-autonomous AI only on interceptor drones, because adding AI to ordinary FPVs significantly raises cost, and it is better to buy several more without AI. But he predicts AI technology will spread quickly and prices will fall, making future battlefields even more brutal.

item.title: The Wow! Signal Hasn't Been Settled in Nearly 50 Years: It Looks Like an Alien Call, but No Second Call Ever Came
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-isaacarthur-wow信号近50年没落定-它像外星呼叫-却再没来第二声/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-isaacarthur-wow信号近50年没落定-它像外星呼叫-却再没来第二声/
item.description: That 72-second narrowband hydrogen-line signal from 1977 has never repeated, and it falls short of the threshold for evidence of an alien civilization; its legacy isn't an answer but a reminder: in a noisy universe, the distance between detection and proof spans an entire galaxy.
item.content:encoded:
That 72-second narrowband hydrogen-line signal from 1977 has never repeated, and it falls short of the threshold for evidence of an alien civilization; its legacy isn't an answer but a reminder: in a noisy universe, the distance between detection and proof spans an entire galaxy.

Anyone hoping for a verdict will be disappointed; anyone wanting to understand how a single anomaly becomes evidence or fails to, this episode offers a complete framework for judging it.

3:09 The 72-second length comes from Earth's rotation
Big Ear was a transit telescope: it didn't turn to track a target, it let Earth's rotation sweep the whole sky overhead. A point source fixed on the celestial sphere crossing the beam naturally takes about 72 seconds — exactly 1/1200 of a day. So the duration doesn't mean the sender deliberately spoke for only 72 seconds; what really matters is the gain curve: a real source enters the beam, strengthens, leaves the beam, weakens. The Wow! signal matched all of it, and any later terrestrial-interference explanation has to clear that bar first.

5:10 6EQUJ5 is an intensity curve, not a code
6EQUJ5 is the signal-strength reading under Big Ear's early print format: each symbol represents an observation window of about 12 seconds, and digits and letters indicate the multiple above background noise. In time order they are 6, 14, 26, 30, 19, 5 — strong in the middle, weak at the ends, like a brightness curve written sideways. Renormalized to 1–100, that's 17, 40, 74, 86, 54, 14. The host's quip is worth remembering: if the aliens' first sentence looks like an invalid software activation code, that's a reasonable opening too.

7:11 Right next to the hydrogen line, yet 50 kHz off
1420 MHz is the radio spectral line of neutral hydrogen, the natural landmark of the universe's most abundant element, and the frequency SETI most often assumes a call would use. Because Big Ear had its master oscillator set 0.1 MHz high, the Wow! signal's frequency has two corrected figures: 1420.356 MHz or 1420.456 MHz; the true hydrogen line sits at about 1420.406 MHz. Both are only about 50 kHz off, as if deliberately avoiding hydrogen noise while using the hydrogen line as a coordinate. But that spot is also full of natural hydrogen-cloud signal sources, and cleverness can't be distinguished from coincidence by frequency alone.

11:13 One horn received it, the other didn't
Big Ear had two feed horns side by side. A source fixed on the celestial sphere, swept by Earth's rotation, should enter the two horns in succession and be recorded twice. The Wow! signal appeared in only one horn, and the records don't say which, so the sky retains two candidate positions. Possible reasons include: the source itself lit up only briefly, a narrow beam happened to graze past, or the interference came from nearby. Every later search — including the 2022 Breakthrough Listen hunt for sun-like stars in the candidate region with Green Bank and the Allen array — heard no repeat. The missing second detection is the core reason it can't make the confirmed list.

15:17 Terrestrial interference and satellites are both hard to mimic
Earth is noisy, but a genuine candidate signal has to pass the 72-second profile test: an ordinary aircraft crossing the beam wouldn't take so conveniently long; a low-orbit satellite usually sweeps past in just seconds. For a satellite to do it, it would need to be in high orbit, leaking through a side lobe, or on a special trajectory — a whole chain of coincidences. Terrestrial transmissions are banned in the internationally protected 1420 MHz band, but illegal equipment or faulty electronics could produce out-of-band signals that leak in through an antenna side lobe. There's also an effect called interstellar scintillation that can briefly brighten a distant signal, but that requires an amplified source to exist first. None of these explanations is perfect, which is exactly why the puzzle survives.

19:18 A magnetar could pump a hydrogen cloud into a maser
Research drawing on Arecibo archives has produced a natural explanation: some high-energy transient — a magnetar flare, say — pumps atoms in a cold neutral hydrogen cloud into a population inversion, briefly turning the cloud into a natural maser in the radio band, much as a laser amplifies microwaves. This can explain several things at once: the signal came from space, sat near the hydrogen line, was strong enough, yet appeared only once; the hydrogen cloud was glowing as the first horn swept past, and had gone dark by the time the second horn came around. The host says this is his personal favorite, because it solves multiple problems within a single mechanism, but it remains a speculative path with no conclusive evidence.

27:27 Becoming a discovery means passing four gates
If a signal like this arrives again, calling it a true technosignature would require at least four conditions: one, it repeats at the same position, so we know it's still there; two, telescopes at two different locations receive it simultaneously, ruling out Earth interference; three, the signal carries modulation, encoding, or mathematical structure, rather than being a bare carrier; four, known natural processes are ruled out one by one. Historically, when pulsars were first discovered they were nicknamed "little green men," showing that nature can perfectly impersonate intelligence. The right posture isn't to pick a side between belief and mockery, but to allow excitement and then do everything possible to prove you're fooling yourself.

31:29 Its legacy is a window that was far too narrow
The Wow! signal appeared for 72 seconds in exactly the form early SETI hoped to recognize — narrowband, near the hydrogen line, strong enough, shaped like a real source in the sky — and then nothing more. It showed what a great discovery might look like before it has gathered enough evidence. The host's landing point: the galaxy is 100,000 light-years wide and billions of years old, and even the largest civilization is just one flickering spark within it. If civilizations don't spread, don't transmit often, and don't often point a beam at us, the Fermi paradox may not exist. With that 1/1200 of a day, the Wow! signal briefly put that possibility in front of humanity.

item.title: Land Is Not a Commodity: Why a Land Value Tax Can Cure the Housing Crisis
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.description: The housing shortage is only a symptom; the real disease is land monopoly. A land value tax shifts the burden off buildings and onto land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, and returning location value to society instead of fattening landlords.
item.content:encoded:
The housing shortage is only a symptom; the real disease is land monopoly. A land value tax shifts the burden off buildings and onto land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, and returning location value to society instead of fattening landlords.

The land value tax is an overlooked lever that economists on both left and right agree on. Lars Doucet turns an abstract tax regime into a power struggle, using Houston parking lots, South Korea's appraisal system, and Norway's resource dividend as cases.

0:05 A land tax is not a property tax, it is a location tax
Lars builds his case on an analogy: the land value tax and the ordinary property tax share an origin, but the LVT splits ‘building value’ from ‘land value’. A building tax punishes you for constructing, maintaining, and renovating; a land tax only punishes you for occupying a good location and letting nothing grow on it. He says land value comes from the labor of the people around you — your ability to earn a living, go to school, and make friends the moment you walk out the door depends entirely on your neighbors and the whole city. The landlord lies back and sucks this collective value into his own pocket, and that is the paradox of Progress and Poverty: the ballpoint pen fell from $270 to 11 cents, but land never does.

0:13 The builders are right, but not right enough
The host asks: Auckland upzoned and rents fell, so do we still need a land tax? Lars concedes that ‘housing shortage’ is the main cause, but points out that YIMBYs never explain a counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet its downtown still holds a giant surface parking lot worth $500 million. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and building together, so the more you build the more tax you pay, while sitting on it and waiting for appreciation is cheaper. So developers have no incentive to develop, only an incentive to lobby for rezoning and then keep hoarding. He says reform without a land tax ends in a stalemate: ‘you changed the zoning, but I just won't sell.’

0:23 The objections run on imagination
Lars sorts the opposition into three camps and takes them apart one by one. How do you appraise land separately from buildings? He says 14,000 appraisal jurisdictions worldwide already do something like it; South Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample parcels a year and produces nationwide land values in 5 months; Norway trained a national automated valuation model on the state property data platform Finn.no with a core team of just 3 people. Think there will be too many protests? He says the real source of protest is ‘the land looks the same as next door, why charge me more’ — under a land tax, you and your neighbor are appraised on the same location basis, which actually makes it easier. The excuse for not doing it is that nobody has measured it.

0:35 The little old lady is not an argument
The sharpest criticism is ‘the transition is unfair’ — on the day a land tax is announced, existing landlords instantly bear the capitalized burden of all future taxes, which amounts to expropriation in one stroke. Lars concedes this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers safeguards: the move is never a one-step nationwide 100% land tax, but a gradual switchover by school district or county; run revenue-neutral simulations and most single-family homes actually see their tax bill fall. As for the elderly afraid of being driven out of their old homes, he says Texas already has a tax deferral system: owe it now, and it is deducted with interest from the estate after death.

0:41 Britain's failure was a capacity problem
The most-cited counterexample online is Britain's 1910s ‘People's Budget’: the valuation took 6 years and was overturned by shopkeepers' protests and the courts. Lars's response is blunt: that viral article is simply ‘deriving a universal law from one sample’, and it simultaneously claims that ‘a pure land tax has never succeeded’ and that ‘land cannot be valued’ — yet South Korea has been appraising nationwide land values parcel by parcel for decades. He says this only proves the British state machine was weak, not that a land tax is theoretically unworkable. His tone hardens: if you want to be a serious critic, go find counterexamples, instead of passing off lazy ignorance as a verdict.

0:45 Norway achieves Georgism through a resource dividend
Lars points to a fact that makes Norway a ‘success story’ today: the entire Norwegian resource management regime is Georgist in structure — oil and other natural resources are deemed the property of all the people, and extractors pay extremely high resource taxes, but production and investment themselves are not punished, so entrepreneurship is encouraged while the natural bounty is captured for the treasury and funds universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except that it is not on land value. This ‘Norwegian paradox’ leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state, it can be its foundation.

0:51 The automobile opened a second frontier
Lars explains why the land question that obsessed every city 100 years ago later vanished: the frontier itself is a mechanism of ‘free land’ — as long as you can still expand into the wilderness, the poor never have to face the squeeze of ‘high wages plus high rent’. America's first frontier was westward expansion, and when it closed, Henry George appeared; in the 20th century the automobile turned the suburbs into a ‘second frontier’ that lasted another 80 years, until it closed again around 2006-2008. He says people now call this a ‘second Gilded Age’, but it is just the script from a hundred years ago with a new cast, and post-pandemic remote work, as a ‘third frontier’, held out for about 5 minutes before capital digested it.

0:53 Don't win online, do the politicians' homework
The closing answer is very practical: Lars says the most effective way to create change he has learned in the past 5 years is not arguing with keyboard warriors, but taking every objection a state senator or city council member might raise, running the data simulations and preparing the answers in advance, and putting them directly on their desks — he calls ‘doing politicians' homework’ an absurd but extraordinarily effective strategy. Several states have already passed bills allowing land value tax reform. His call to action: go measure, don't guess.

item.title: What Drives Founders Isn't Becoming a Billionaire, It's the Fear of the Server Crashing at 3 A.M.
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-ycsp-驱动创始人的不是当亿万富翁-是怕服务器半夜崩掉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-ycsp-驱动创始人的不是当亿万富翁-是怕服务器半夜崩掉/
item.description: Most people assume it's wealth ambition that carries founders through. Paul Graham says what actually pushes people forward day to day is disaster fear — the server goes down, the model train is about to fall off the table; you keep your head down for ten years, look up, do the math, and realize that at the last round's valuation you're already a billionaire.
item.content:encoded:
Most people assume it's wealth ambition that carries founders through. Paul Graham says what actually pushes people forward day to day is disaster fear — the server goes down, the model train is about to fall off the table; you keep your head down for ten years, look up, do the math, and realize that at the last round's valuation you're already a billionaire.

After 21 years and 47 batches, PG's judgment: AI has changed almost nothing about startups, only the bill. Useful for calibrating your confidence in "this time is different."

2:02 People nostalgic for the golden age forget the only hit was Reddit
Since roughly 2008 people have been saying YC is finished — PG's read is that its attackers have to first admit it was once great, so all they can ever say is "not as good as it used to be." But his counterexample is concrete: the flagship of the supposed good old days was Reddit, while the projects he did office hours with this episode include intercontinental ballistic freight — like an ICBM, except it doesn't explode on landing, it unloads. Another category is curing cancer. He says there are too many ways to go at this — a vaccine at one end, therapies at the other — so you should fund several; any one that works is worth it. This episode had a company doing on-demand research for cancer patients, and what he liked was exactly that approach: cancer is famously not solved by "coming up with a cure," and maybe the way to beat it is death by a thousand cuts.

4:09 Google won't be breached, it will be made obsolete by the world
Many of the ideas in the 2012 "frighteningly ambitious" list have already been done, and one of them was "the new Google." PG says he predicted the path back then: you can't attack Google head-on, you can only wait for the day the world changes enough that its model goes out of date. OpenAI is that change itself — after using it he found he no longer uses search, because what he always wanted wasn't web pages, it was information, so he just asks the AI. This is a corollary that holds for every incumbent: a moat isn't breached, it's made obsolete.

6:15 Ambition is the ticket in; the daily fuel is fear of looking like an idiot
Ambition is a necessity, because the obstacles in startups are too terrifying to push through on conscientiousness alone. But PG says what actually gets a founder moving at any given moment isn't "if I solve this I'll become a billionaire," it's disaster fear: the server is down, the fear of looking like a fool. His image is a toy train — the engine is going off the edge of the table and you lunge to catch it. You keep your head down fixing that train for ten years, look up, do the math on the last round's valuation, and discover you're already a billionaire. He says sometimes he's the one who does the math first and tells the founder.

9:21 The only test of formidable is whether they get what they want
Formidable is a private word PG and Jessica were using before YC. His definition is operational: this person gets what they want in any situation — if they can't, what does formidable even mean. That definition incidentally explains the investing logic: you hold stock in his company, he holds it too, interests are aligned; he gets what he wants, you get what you want. It's also the precondition for his answer to "where does the next trillion-dollar company come from."

11:24 Lean startup isn't dead: even rocket companies can start small
Asked whether lean startup is dead and whether you now have to burn big money from day one, PG's rebuttal has two layers. First, price: tokens are expensive now only because of the GPU shortage, and the price for the same level of inference will fall by roughly 30x a year — plus you're getting higher-quality tokens — technology always gets cheaper. Second, path: even rocket companies can start with not much money; you can't build a real rocket, but you can build the design, run simulations, show it to experts, and if it's convincing enough you get the next round. StarCloud wrote a white paper and booked a launch — though he adds that that founder was already a well-known expert in the field with built-in credibility; a fresh graduate doesn't have it that easy.

13:24 AI went the wrong direction: from human toward perfect
People doing AI in the 1980s thought the path started from "the perfect fly": able to do only what a fly does, but as well as a fly does it; then climb up to mouse, cat, monkey, human, each level perfect. What we got was the reverse — a complete human right out of the gate, just talking nonsense, like an undergrad trying to bluff his way through a paper. The dimension being optimized was the opposite one: not from perfect toward human, but from human toward perfect. This also explains the jagged frontier: it can solve hard math problems but can't tell you what time a restaurant opens.

16:30 AI changes the bill structure, not the shipping speed
PG says the best predictor of startup success is still shipping speed, and AI hasn't replaced that metric — with these tools in hand, plenty of companies this episode still weren't shipping fast enough, which shows the difference isn't how fast you can write code; you first have to come up with the ideas. "With AI, what's still unchanged?" His answer: so far almost everything is exactly the same. The only strange new thing is the bill structure — the biggest cost of a startup used to be salaries, everything else was cheap by comparison; now there's GPUs on top, and tokens can burn tens of thousands of dollars a day.

19:36 The next trillion-dollar company comes from the right person, not the right idea
Asked where the next trillion-dollar company will come from, PG swaps the question from sector to person outright: it comes from the right founder, not some particular idea — startup ideas are highly variable, and all he'll say is "probably not dog-walking." Conversely, to judge whether a company is worth investing in, first judge whether the founder is formidable; what they're working on is probably promising. As for whether future founders will look different, he says there are already 20 years of data, today's founders are exactly the same as 20 years ago, and there's no reason the next 20 years will be different.

item.title: Arm Moves Into Building CPUs: The Biggest Bottleneck in Chip Design Is Verification, Not Design
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.description: The real time sink in a chip cycle is verification, debug and documentation, not RTL; 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily, and Arm is breaking its 98.5%-gross-margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.
item.content:encoded:
The real time sink in a chip cycle is verification, debug and documentation, not RTL; 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily, and Arm is breaking its 98.5%-gross-margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.

It uses real internal Arm data to explain what AI actually does for chip design, then ties product, capital and supply-chain judgments into one closed loop — worth checking against your own expectations if you work in AI infrastructure.

3:43 Arm is building CPUs itself because customers are pushing it to
Arm used to sell only IP licenses at 98.5% gross margin, never touching inventory or wafers. One step forward, the compute subsystem already had customers grabbing pre-assembled CPU, GPU and memory "subsystems" as modules; the next step forward came because "customers who want a general-purpose CPU for the large-model era can't find a supplier" and went straight to Arm to push for one. Before announcing, Arm asked nearly every license customer, and opposition was minimal: a bigger software ecosystem benefits every customer, so Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft and Google — all companies building Arm server chips — publicly supported it.

8:07 Banning AI tools is sending engineers back to the library
A full chip design cycle runs 24-36 months; the biggest time sink is not RTL generation or architecture mapping but verification, validation, debug and documentation. AI is especially well suited to those steps, and roughly 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily; turning the tools off is like telling people in the 1990s they could use the internet only two hours a day and had to go back downstairs to the library for the rest. Where AI is currently weakest is RTL generation and physical design, because models depend on public corpora while the industry's most critical details are private data — exactly the gap companies like Arm can fill.

10:35 From idea to layout is five years away, not two or three
The host asked: once AI eats verification, the most time-consuming step, can 24-36 months shrink to 6-12? Rene Haas gave a measured answer: 2-3 years is unrealistic; five-plus years, for designs with not-too-complex constraints, going from idea all the way to GDSII (the layout file handed to the fab) is possible. If you type into the tool "make a chip 10% faster, 20% cheaper and 30% more power-efficient than some reference," don't expect one-click completion. His judgment is that in 5-10 years the whole industry's design methodology will visibly change.

15:00 AI supply and demand are still far apart, and the bottleneck is the construction site, not the wafer
On the AI bubble, Rene Haas says you have to separate valuation froth at the stock level from the supply chain itself; he states plainly that supply is still "far" from demand. Transformer inference and training eat both compute and memory, and demand won't stop. The real hard constraint will shift to data center construction: many projects are running late and need more hands, and resistance limiting new data center builds is appearing in various places; over the next 3-5 years the binding constraint may not be wafer capacity or memory but the physical build-out staying perpetually tight.

17:14 SoftBank doing cloud is about being a customer for chip companies
For capital-heavy, capex-intensive chip/AI founders: capital availability is itself the gate, and strategic partnerships need to reach early into three layers — supply chain, PE and banks. Behind Arm is SoftBank, and not just as a shareholder; SoftBank has just announced it will build a "neo cloud"-style cloud service, which lets young chip companies avoid only knocking on Microsoft's or Google's door for a design win and instead form a direct customer relationship with the Arm/SoftBank ecosystem — one more path to deployment.

21:25 Humanoids won't unify everything; specialized robots will coexist long-term
Rene Haas sees robot 1.0 as purpose-built: both mechanics and software optimized for a single motion, so changing a production line means nearly starting over. A new generation of robots that can redefine tasks through training, with mechanical bodies that are also general-purpose, will first eat repetitive labor in construction, infrastructure and security. Form factor won't go in a single direction: factories, warehouses and tools are all designed to human dimensions, so humanoids have an advantage; another set of tasks is better served by specialized forms. Cost has to come down first, and delivery and warehousing will be the earliest automated scenarios.

27:13 Restricting chips to China is an unwinnable infinite game
On US manufacturing he is direct: the US should build more fabs at home, needed both for national security and for supply-chain diversification. On export controls, he frames it as an "infinite game" — restricting chips to China cannot produce a victory with an end state, and may instead push critical technology out of the US. He also rejects the idea that data centers are "big warehouses with no jobs": energy, liquid cooling and the surrounding ecosystem are all jobs that can be created in the US.

36:00 In a token world, every path runs through a CPU
If you use the token factory metaphor for accelerators, Rene Haas thinks the real system question is: who orchestrates and arbitrates where those tokens go, and delivers them to users. He believes every path runs through a CPU: beyond training, there's inference scheduling, system orchestration, context and tool calls. At the edge, on devices that can't host a 50W GPU, Arm's power advantage is even more pronounced. The CPU hasn't disappeared — it's forming persistent demand alongside accelerators.

item.title: The Number One Fraud Red Flag Isn't Greed — It's a Personal Financial Breakdown
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/

item.description: For 14 straight years, ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a critical brain region going offline, and moral overconfidence all let good people cross the line step by step.
item.content:encoded:
For 14 straight years, ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a critical brain region going offline, and moral overconfidence all let good people cross the line step by step.

One author is a clinical neuropsychologist, the other has 20 years of experience suing financial advisors; the offender profiles and warning signals here have more screening value than moral slogans.

2:04 The only test for crossing the line: "This is not your money"
Moira defines financial misconduct as "doing bad things with other people's money": it includes both taking the money for yourself and guiding or advising others to deploy funds in ways that aren't in their best interest. She stresses that anyone working in finance must always remember "this is not your money." Reducing the ethical question to fiduciary duty gives all the later warning signals a single baseline for judgment.

9:10 The number one red flag for 14 straight years is personal financial problems
Philippa cites ACFE's global report: for 14 consecutive years, the top fraud red flag has not been greed but "personal financial problems" — people whose personal finances are out of control, who can't make ends meet, or who are drowning in debt are the most likely to get involved in financial misconduct. The financial industry offers access to other people's money, attracts people who chase wealth, and is layered on top of people's irrationality around money — three conditions stacked into fertile ground for misconduct.

13:14 Listening to advice, the brain acts like it's praying: the critical region goes offline
Moira notes that neuroimaging evidence shows that when people receive financial advice, key critical regions of the brain go "offline," in a state similar to the brain during prayer. People feel safe, trusting, and open, and this non-critical state heightens vulnerability, especially for those unfamiliar with finance. She gives the example that even hedge fund managers will "sit and wait for the answer" in front of an advisor rather than pressing on how a product actually works.

19:19 Good people start erring through obedience and eagerness to help, not greed
Philippa and Moira break down the path by which good people err: blindly obeying orders, crossing the line out of "misguided helpfulness," then hiding the mistake out of fear, then covering it with a bigger lie. The book's "John" slides from a small slip into lying, then into doubling down on the cover-up. Moira stresses that ethics is not a solo sport but a team sport; if the organizational culture tacitly permits misconduct, it's very hard for an individual to stay clean on their own.

37:36 Psychopaths flow into finance disproportionately
Responding to Cameron's concern, Moira says the evidence shows psychopaths flow disproportionately into finance and business because "that's where the money is." She cites Robert Hare's research: successful psychopaths tend to be charming and are extremely good at detecting and exploiting other people's desires. The damage they do is large, and they often keep circulating within the industry because colleagues feel a sense of "relief" when they leave, leaving the problem for the next firm.

53:50 Most people don't realize they're making an ethical decision at all
Traditional ethics training always presents clear moral dilemmas in a classroom, but real-world problems tend to emerge quietly, so people don't realize they're at a fork in the road. Moira cites Kahneman's "what you see is all there is": people don't proactively question the motives of product providers, don't think about who benefits from a complex product, and don't admit to themselves that they don't actually understand it. The result is that even with ethics training, most of the time they have no idea they're facing an ethical decision.

1:02:56 The future wrongdoer is a vulnerable ordinary person, not a bad guy
Philippa lists the profile of the future wrongdoer: early in their career (Evan got swept into a global fraud one month into the job and was banned for life nine months later), in debt, highly dependent on their boss, a people-pleaser, low self-esteem (compensated for with a luxury car), fatigued, dealing with family problems, and so on. These signals are rarely used by the industry to screen advisors for their own biases; they aren't some rare evil but the common weaknesses of ordinary people under pressure and vulnerability.

1:09:07 After 20 years of suing, she has never sued a single CFP
Philippa practiced law for 20 years and sued many financial professionals, but never once sued a CFP certificant. She believes there's no simple way to pick out a good advisor, but holding a certification is a positive signal. She also offers a test: if an advisor only talks about investments and doesn't understand the client's whole life situation, that's just wealth management, not financial planning — the object of planning is the person, not the assets.

item.title: The 5% Treasury Yield Isn't About Inflation: $32 Trillion of Debt Means Buyers Will Only Take More at a Higher Price
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.description: Inflation can't explain a 30-year above 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, a buyer already fully allocated at 5.3% won't budge for another $10 billion. What's really steepening the curve is $2 trillion of new Treasury supply every year, and buybacks can't hold it down.
item.content:encoded:
Inflation can't explain a 30-year above 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, a buyer already fully allocated at 5.3% won't budge for another $10 billion. What's really steepening the curve is $2 trillion of new Treasury supply every year, and buybacks can't hold it down.

The mainstream narrative pins the 30-year at 5% on inflation; this episode offers a genuinely incremental alternative framework and folds the limits of Treasury intervention, the mechanics of Fed balance-sheet runoff, and the term premium debate into one logic.

4:04 5% is first the Treasury's interest bill, not a macro signal
Host Joe asks Daryl what he sees when the 30-year Treasury yield is above 5% — even after it ticked down slightly that day following the Fed chair's remarks. Daryl's answer isn't a macro model but the Treasury's predicament: if I were the Treasury secretary, what I'd see is that US government interest expense is extraordinarily high, and I'd have to find a way to push yields down. That line sets the frame for the whole episode: the official side has a strong motive to push long-end rates down, but whether it can and whether it should are the premises for everything that follows.

5:07 The Treasury wants to sell another $10 billion, and can only pay more
Daryl gives the single most important thought experiment of the segment: suppose there's no inflation risk and no sovereign default, and you're a macro hedge fund that already holds $20 billion of 10-year Treasuries. The Treasury secretary calls and asks you to buy another $10 billion — why won't you? The answer: at a 5.3% yield you've already made the allocation you want, and to get you to add, you'd have to be paid a higher rate as compensation. This logic incidentally explains the structural shift on the demand side — foreign central banks are long since fully allocated and no longer buying, so new Treasury supply can only land on domestic free discretionary buyers: banks, pensions, insurers, hedge funds, and that money is highly sensitive to yield.

8:10 The logic didn't change; the debt stock hit a tipping point
Joe raises the objection that has to be faced: aging populations, a political system with no appetite for spending cuts, unsustainable deficits — this bearish logic existed in 2018 and 2019, and Japan was talked about this way for decades before that, so why did yields keep falling then and why are they rising now? Daryl's answer is a scale effect: the 60% debt/GDP red line the IMF drew back then is far behind us, France is already at 100%; the US Treasury market grew from roughly $18 trillion to $31 trillion and keeps expanding. There's no new logic — the quantity of debt itself has accumulated to a tipping point.

10:13 The long end's 5% is mostly issuance, not inflation expectations
Since the short end is still pinned by high inflation and the Fed, why not attribute the high 30-year yield directly to inflation expectations? Daryl concedes inflation over the past five years has indeed been well above the Fed's target and the job of getting back to target isn't done, but points out: implied inflation expectations backed out of real versus nominal bonds are not flashing alarm; the investors actually buying and selling 10-, 20- and 30-year Treasuries are not processing inflation first in their heads — they're processing supply relative to demand. He mentions John Cochrane's fiscal theory of the price level, but that's a long-run framework — the main driver of today's term premium is issuance, not prices.

13:18 Buybacks to cap yields are just a signal, with far too little ammunition
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an expansion of Treasury buybacks, with liquidity as the official rationale. Daryl reads the subtext directly: from the wording of his public remarks, he doesn't think the problem is market liquidity — he thinks yields are ‘too high’, and he says outright that he's sending a signal to the market. The problem is that the size of Treasury's operations is a drop in the bucket relative to the whole Treasury market, and the market moved briefly on the news and then reversed quickly. Trying to use the government's own resources to suppress the path of yields has a precedent in the 1992 sterling crisis — and Bessent was the man shorting the pound at Soros's fund.

19:22 Buybacks' real job is sweeping up old bonds, not managing rates
The buyback program wasn't originally designed to manage yields: as the Treasury keeps issuing new securities, a large stock of illiquid off-the-run old bonds is left in the market, clogging dealer balance sheets and trading away from a smooth yield curve. A paper Daryl is working on with two New York Fed economists is testing whether sweeping up the fragments on a ‘regular, predictable’ schedule and swapping in new issues can improve market liquidity and earn taxpayers the gain from buying low and selling high. The phrase ‘odd lots’ happens to be where the show's name comes from. He thinks this routine operation works; the Treasury stepping in at a moment of emergency to defend its own bond market is a different matter.

25:30 The constraint on runoff is reserves, not the asset side
A new Fed chair may want to shrink the balance sheet, but most people only stare at the asset side. Daryl points to the arithmetic constraint: selling assets requires extinguishing an equal amount of liabilities. Of the three liability blocks, the TGA can't have the Treasury pull its deposits out, circulating currency can't be recalled, and the only thing that can be squeezed is commercial banks' reserves at the Fed. But today's reserves are the ‘Swiss Army knife of the financial industry’: they pay interest at market rates, satisfy liquidity regulation, and are usable for payments at any moment, so banks have no incentive to give them up. The ratchet effect that Acharya and Rajan laid out at Jackson Hole in 2017 already showed this: every time the Fed expands its balance sheet, banks get addicted to reserves, and shrinking it necessarily causes market volatility.

28:33 The task force will swap duration, not actually shrink the size
Daryl states he has no inside information on the task force, but makes two predictions about the group led by Jeremy Stein: first, the real problem isn't size but composition, and the sensible move is to gradually replace the Fed's long-dated Treasuries with short-term bills, so that reserve interest expense on the liability side offsets bill interest income on the asset side in the same direction, reducing the hit to the Fed's own P&L from swings in the policy rate; second, don't keep mortgage-backed securities on the asset side — let them roll off naturally. His own conclusion is blunter: the Fed doesn't necessarily have to shrink the balance sheet, but it must have the tools in hand to shrink it on its own, or it will be backed into a corner when Congress applies pressure.
