item.description: ResNet is the most cited paper of the 21st century, but its real contribution is not making networks deeper — it invented the residual stream, a kind of working memory that lets a model store and edit information, and that changed how we understand neural networks entirely.
item.content:encoded:
ResNet is the most cited paper of the 21st century, but its real contribution is not making networks deeper — it invented the residual stream, a kind of working memory that lets a model store and edit information, and that changed how we understand neural networks entirely.

This episode uses clear animations and experiments to explain why residual connections work, how they gave rise to the Transformer, and the evidence that the residual stream acts as working memory. Suited to anyone who wants to understand the essence of modern AI architecture in depth.

2:07 Deeper networks perform worse, not better
In early 2015, Sun Jian's team used careful initialization to push a network to 30 layers, but performance got worse than 14 layers (error rate 16.59% vs 13.34%). In theory, a 30-layer model could match a 14-layer one at minimum via identity mappings, but the optimizer cannot find such a solution. This hints the problem is not network capacity but the training process itself.

15:18 Shattered gradients are the root disease of deep networks
By visualizing the loss landscape, they found that as layers increase, the loss surface of early layers becomes extremely rugged and gradient directions become as random as white noise — this is called the "shattered gradients problem." Gradients are the core signal of learning; once they fail, deep networks cannot be trained effectively.

17:18 Residual connections: an almost absurdly simple fix
Sun Jian's team's solution was laughably simple: between every two layers, add the input tensor directly to the output, forming a skip connection. This gives activations and gradients a direct path and effectively eliminates the shattered gradients problem. A 74-layer network with skip connections jumped from 38.9% to 72.6% accuracy, sweeping the major 2015 vision competitions.

20:19 ResNet overturns the theory of hierarchical representations
A Cornell team found that deleting or even shuffling ResNet's layers has little effect on performance. This contradicted the then-mainstream theory of hierarchical representations — the idea that each layer builds on the previous one, so deleting any layer should be catastrophic. It forced the field to rethink: ResNet may not be learning hierarchical features but iteratively refining a "residual stream" that runs through the whole network.

26:26 The residual stream: modern AI's hidden backbone
Straighten out the skip connections and you see an unbroken stream of data from input to output, with each layer only making incremental edits on top. This "residual stream" later became the core design of the Transformer and a cornerstone of modern AI. But note: follow-up work shows ResNet learns hierarchical representations and refines the residual stream at the same time — the two can coexist.

29:28 The residual stream is the model's working memory
A Meta team found that in a vision Transformer's residual stream, activations at certain positions are unusually large and concentrated in unimportant regions of the image. They hypothesized the model treats these positions as "registers" to aggregate global information. Experiments confirmed it: the embeddings at these high-activation positions perform astonishingly well on image classification (85.2% vs 10.8%), and once extra "register tokens" are added, the model no longer occupies image positions.

item.content:encoded:
The Fed's credibility broke over a single decision not to hike, yet the options market still prices Fed days like any other day — the cheapest insurance may be an illusion.

Three pieces of evidence — sticky inflation, the midterms, and Fed credibility — point at the same thing: volatility is too low and cheap protection is a mirage. The framework and the data are both concrete.

3:03 A Fed without forward guidance is flipping a coin
The two hosts open by pointing at what has changed: in past FOMC meetings the market knew the odds with near certainty in advance, whereas this time the probability of a hike at the next meeting is only 55 to 45 — barely better than a coin flip. Add Warsh's Jackson Hole statement that he wants to fade forward guidance, and every meeting from here can turn into ‘wait for the outcome, then react’. Rate surprises transmit through debt and leverage into every asset, so volatility has to be repriced. The hosts also assert, based on history, that once the market truly tests them, almost every official eventually capitulates — so this current commitment to ‘never give the market expectations in advance’ is itself the most testable variable.

17:31 Midterm volatility is priced as just another day
Kevin Muir thinks midterm volatility is badly underpriced. During the 2022 midterms, the options market priced a single-day S&P move of ±1.8% for voting day; in 2018 it was ±1.25%; now it is only ±0.9%. And this time Trump's approval is at historic lows, and he just spent an hour in a primetime address talking about ‘election fraud’, as if paving the way to challenge the result. Muir is careful to say: it's fine if you think he's overthinking it — as voting day approaches, the question of whether the election will be disrupted will itself get repriced. With volatility near seasonal lows and implied correlation also at historic lows, the odds on being long volatility are far better than usual.

23:41 The inflation pullback is a supply illusion; demand hasn't cooled
Ahan Manon breaks the PCE components into ‘demand-driven’ and ‘supply-driven’. Right now the contributions are 3.31 versus 0.38; even if you strip out the energy supply shock from the Iran situation entirely, the remaining demand side alone is enough to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target. Historically, demand-driven inflation is slow and persistent, while supply-driven inflation tends to spike fast and mean-revert within 6 to 12 months. The breadth is the bigger problem: in recent months, 70% to 80% of PCE components rose more than 2%. June briefly went negative month-over-month and July only rebounded 16 basis points, but that short-term cooling came almost entirely from the supply side; the demand-driven trend was never interrupted.

34:51 One hike could have fixed the credibility; he didn't do it
Ben Hunt says Warsh shot himself in the foot at the press conference after the July meeting. Earlier, the new face and the hawkish inflation talk had repaired the ‘Fed credibility’ narrative substantially; but what was actually needed was an immediate 25 basis point hike. Do that once, and the market believes ‘he does what he says’, and you never need to hike repeatedly afterward. Skip that step and the narrative flips completely: every independent piece that appeared in the financial media that week, in different words, said the same thing — ‘meet the new boss, same as the old boss’. Once credibility shatters it is hard to glue back; the August gold rally was precisely the market's response to ‘hawkish talk, no action’.

40:13 After credibility is damaged, only verbal financial repression is left
Ben Hunt lists four pressures the Fed and Treasury must handle but absolutely cannot let blow up: the Iran war has no easy exit and oil stays higher for longer; fiscal stimulus effects fade and tariff pressure returns; the insurance sector has a systemic problem of captive insurers being used to warehouse private investments; and 10-year and 30-year long-end yields above all cannot be pushed higher by the market. Any one of these could be the fuse for the next financial crisis. Handling them requires credibility, and credibility has just been damaged, so every policy option left is ‘verbal financial repression’ — using statements and intervention to hold yields down rather than letting the market price them. His judgment: this operation has no maturity date, it only accelerates.

49:25 The options market treats a Fed meeting like any other day
The options term structure Brent Kachuba shows has almost no event risk: on the day of Warsh's speech, the S&P 0DTE straddle was worth only 38 index points; SPX options expiring August 31 carried implied volatility of just 7%, the overall term structure sat at a 90-day low, and put open interest was very low. He normally avoids trading Fed events, because events turn options into a kind of ‘tax’ — you collect premium before the event, and time value decays the moment it passes. What's special this time is that the market has crushed expected volatility to near zero and nobody is buying protection; before Jackson Hole he bought a few ‘lottery tickets’ with extremely cheap short-dated put spreads, because if Warsh says one thing the market doesn't want to hear, naked option sellers get flattened instantly. Once the event passes is a better time to chase directional trends.

58:42 Outsource the writing and you outsource the thinking
The closing topic is the Druckenmiller column handed to the WSJ: he openly said it was written with AI, for the simple reason that AI writes better than he does. The two hosts argue the core question is whether the views and the emotion belong to the author; Druckenmiller's piece reads like his usual intuitive judgment, with AI only organizing and expressing it, so it isn't deception. Ben Hunt draws the line at the writing itself: writing is part of the thinking process, ‘I write it down to figure out what I think’. When the text-generation step is outsourced, readers lose an important clue — whether the author actually thought these words through. Investment blogs are already full of obvious AI output; judging whether an opinion is reliable can't rest on whether the prose is pretty, but on whether the view has a thinking process behind it.
